en: Advayavajra’s Works 1. *Kudṛṣṭinirghātana*,
edited by Mahāmahopādhyāya Hara Prasad Shastri.
In the *Advayavajrasaṃgraha*, edited by the Mikkyō Seiten Kenkyūkai, Gaekwad’s Oriental Series (GOS) 1927, Baroda;
and in the *Taishō Daigaku Sōgō Bukkyō Kenkyūjo Nenpō* (Annual Report of the Institute for Comprehensive Studies of Buddhism, Taishō University), vol. 10.
*Taishō University Institute of Comprehensive Studies of Buddhism Annuals* 10, 1988, pp. (10/225)–(36/199) % input by Péter-Dániel Szántó
Based on a partial input by Ryūgen Tanemura,
2008 spring vacation, Budapest. Not proofread.
% NB: I have not noted all the similar passages with the Ādikarmapradīpa (cf. p. 1, M 10/225).
Homage to the Buddha!
I shall explain the *Kudṛṣṭinirghāta* according to the rules for beginners;
by this very mode of dwelling and through effort, one attains the state. (1)
For here, beings are of two kinds: those in training (śaikṣa) and those beyond training (aśaikṣa).

Among them, for those in training who abide in the causal stage—characterized by intention, the application of resolute conviction, the application of having entered the stages, and culminating in the attainment of mastery—the attainment of the excellence of perfect enlightenment occurs through the performance of utterly pure actions and so forth, by means of which the two accumulations have been gathered.

Even for those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), who have eliminated all conceptualizations regarding the reality of the antidotes and their fruits, the uninterrupted initial activity characterized by the performance of deeds for the benefit of sentient beings proceeds precisely through the power of the momentum of their previous vows and by means of the yoga of effortless union (*yuganaddha*). Thus it is established.
And so it is said:
"O Protector, you have no conceit, no conceptualization, and no movement."
Without effort, your activity as a Buddha proceeds in the world. || 2 ||
The perfection of the welfare of others is considered the most principal fruit of the Buddhas;
as for Buddhahood and other such qualities, they are regarded as fruits because they have that [perfection] as their purpose. (3)
Like a wish-fulfilling gem, he is unshakable by the winds of all conceptual constructions;
nevertheless, he fulfills the hopes of all sentient beings without exception.

By avoiding both affirmation and negation regarding the factors that oppose the reality of the fruit, the fortunate one awakens to perfect enlightenment; thereafter, however, [he applies himself] to the initial stage of practice. (5)
The fruit [is attained];
that path belongs to the fortunate ones.

Is it not the case that the prescription of initial practice for those in training (*śaikṣa*) is indeed appropriate? How so? Even for those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), who realize the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), there is the commencement of initial practice; this too is merely like being bound by golden shackles. True. [This is so] because of their lack of realization of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*). For the perfection of wisdom is the very essence (*svabhāva*) of the five perfections. Therefore: "Emptiness endowed with the excellence of all aspects is what is proclaimed. (6)
And it was said by the Blessed One:
"The five perfections, when devoid of the perfection of wisdom, do not receive the designation 'perfection'.

And it is said in the *Āryavimalakīrtinirdeśa*: "Skillful means devoid of wisdom is bondage; wisdom devoid of skillful means is bondage. Skillful means accompanied by wisdom is liberation; wisdom accompanied by skillful means is liberation."
And the identity (*tādātmya*) of these two is understood as being spontaneously established (*sahajasiddha*), like that of a lamp and its light, through the instruction of a true guru.
For this very reason—
The initial practice as it has been taught should be performed by all yogins;
that which is desired as the knowledge for enlightenment is the inseparability of emptiness and compassion. (7)
And regarding the initial practice:
"The five perfections are taught under the designation 'initial practice,' yet wisdom-perfection is not intended as their intrinsic nature. (8)
And likewise in this regard:

"The wise person who constantly and respectfully practices generosity, ethical discipline, patience, vigor, meditative concentration, and wisdom becomes happy and remains in a state of well-being. (9)

Generosity, ethical discipline, patience, and meditative concentration are the causes for the Enjoyment Body and the Emanation Body; wisdom is the cause for the Dharma Body; and vigor is considered the cause for both. (10)
Of both.

Therefore, a bodhisattva must be one who dwells in perfectly pure preliminary conduct; otherwise, there would be the consequence of falling into the doctrine of nihilism (*nāstikavāda*). As it has been said:
"Even though the auspicious and the inauspicious are devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvaka*), nevertheless, one should perform only what is auspicious, not what is inauspicious."
In the worldly convention, which is like the reflection of the moon in water,
pleasure is dear and suffering is constantly disliked.

How, then, do those among the *śaikṣas* who abide in the vow of the madman, who possess conviction in non-conceptuality, and who engage in the initial practice [proceed]? It is said: "Having performed the gift of the body, he engaged in the conduct.
(HeTa I.vi.19) And having given the gift of the body, one should thereafter commence the conduct. (12)
Because of this statement:
"Giving is that which is given until the end of the body.
Morality (*śīla*) arises from the restraint of body, speech, and mind for the sake of all sentient beings.
Patience consists in enduring blows such as those from cruel, heated saws; vigor consists in enduring the affliction of the eight worldly dharmas;
and meditative concentration consists in flowing spontaneously and effortlessly, following the nature of all things.

And wisdom consists in the realization of the characteristic of the non-apprehension of all phenomena. When one is permeated by the flavor of effortless spontaneity, all the supreme perfections proceed continuously and without interruption.
While Ś considered this to be a lacunose verse, M takes it as prose:
"Therefore, even for those established in the vow of madness, the initial action indeed proceeds. (M 16/219)
The speech of the Cārvāka beast, who has lost sight of the next world, is not cited at all because it is entirely illogical.
In that regard, the *poṣadha* is first given by the Bodhisattva to the trainee, and thereafter the ten points of training (*śikṣāpada*). (HeTa II.viii.9)
The tenth training rule (*śikṣāpada*) is the "Instruction in Training" (*śikṣopadeśa*), according to the words of the venerable *Hevajra*: first, indeed, is the granting of the *poṣadha*.
In that regard, it is the training for those in training (*śaikṣa*), the actual training (*bhūtaśaikṣa*).

Pay heed, venerable teacher: I, the lay follower named [so-and-so], go for refuge to the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha, until I reach the seat of enlightenment. Thus a second time, and thus a third time.
(As above, p. 4)

"May you hold me as one who has gone for refuge to the Three, saying so. Pay heed, O Ācārya! I, the lay follower named [so-and-so], from this moment until tomorrow at sunrise, during this interval, abstain from all killing of living beings, taking what is not given, unchaste conduct, as well as divisive speech, falsehood, intoxicants, eating at improper times, using garlands, perfumes, dance, song, and music, and high beds and seats. Today I abstain; I undertake these by means of those eight qualities, according to the *Poṣadha-gāthā*.

A householder bodhisattva, however, preceded by taking refuge in the Three Jewels, abstains from the five [transgressions]: killing, taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, lying, and the drinking of intoxicants—which is a natural offense—and is endowed with learning and solitude. A householder bodhisattva who has abandoned the ten unwholesome actions, who observes the vows of non-repetition and practices virtuous deeds, should rise during the morning watch, perform cleansing of the face and so forth, and while recollecting the Three Jewels, protect himself through the yoga of the self-mantra *oṃ āḥ hūṃ*.
Thereafter, he should engage in meditation, recitation, praise, and so on, according to his realization.
One should recite the *Nāmasaṃgīti* three times daily as part of the meditative concentration of realization;
following that:
"Oṃ jambhalajalendrāya svāhā. Having recited this one hundred and eight times, one should offer handfuls of water to Jambhala. Then...
Homage to all Buddhas, O Avalokite, who beholds all Tathāgatas! Omb sambhara sambhara hūṃ phaṭ svāhā!

Having thus repeated the mantra seven times, one should visualize that the five grains of rice for the water-offering (*balibhakta*) placed at the base of the door have been filled by five streams of nectar issuing from the five fingers of the extended right hand; these grains were set in motion by Māgadha using a *droṇa* measure. Then, while satisfying all *preta*s and *piśāca*s, one should snap the fingers three times and present the *bodhisattva-bali*.

Now, having meditated upon loving-kindness (*maitrī*) characterized by affection for all sentient beings as if they were one's only son; compassion (*karuṇā*) whose nature is the desire to rescue them from the ocean of *saṃsāra*, which consists of suffering and the causes of suffering; joy (*muditā*) whose great majesty and power shine forth from taking refuge in the Three Jewels; and equanimity (*upekṣā*) characterized by the absence of attachment—[the practitioner], with a mind intent on the welfare of all beings, [should prepare the site] with pure cow dung and pure water.

Saying "Oṃ āḥ vajrarekhe hūṃ," one should prepare a small maṇḍala— either square or any other of the four [shapes]— on the ground consecrated by the maṇḍala-mantra. In its center, upon the pericarp of a multicolored eight-petaled lotus and atop a sun disk, is the one arisen from a blue syllable *hūṃ*, holding the earth-touching mudrā.

[One should meditate on] Akṣobhya; then, in the eastern petal, Vairocana, white in color, produced from the white syllable Oṃ, holding the bodhyagrī mudrā; then, in the southern petal, Ratnasaṃbhava, yellow in color, born from the yellow syllable Trāṃ, holding the varada mudrā; then, in the western petal, Amitābha, red in color, arisen from the red syllable Hrīḥ, holding the samādhi mudrā; and then, in the northern petal, Amoghasiddhi, green in color, born from the green syllable Khaṃ, holding the abhaya mudrā. Having thus visualized them, [one recites]: Oṃ Āḥ Vajrapuṣpe Hūṃ.

Having consecrated [the offerings] with this mantra, one should present everything most pleasing. These five Tathāgatas are clothed in saffron robes, wear uṣṇīṣas, have their heads and faces shaved, and abide upon solar disks. Vairocana is on a supreme lunar disk; the other four face Akṣobhya, while Akṣobhya faces the practitioner.
In front of them, reciting this verse of the Three Refuges as it has been mastered, one should chant: *In this regard, one should recite this verse of the Three Refuges:* *Oṃ.*
Homage to the Buddha, the Teacher; homage to the Dharma, the Protector;
homage to the great Saṅgha—constant homage to all three. (14)
The Three Jewels are my refuge; I confess all my misdeeds; I rejoice in the merit of the world; I set my mind upon the awakening of a Buddha. 15.
Until enlightenment, I go for refuge to the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Supreme Assembly;
I generate the mind of awakening for the sake of accomplishing the welfare of myself and others. (16)
I generate the supreme mind of awakening;
I address all sentient beings:
it is I! It is I!
I invite [them];
I shall practice the desired, excellent conduct of awakening.
May I become a Buddha for the benefit of the world. || 17 ||
Confession of all misdeeds and rejoicing in all merits; I shall observe the fast, the noble eightfold poṣadha. 18.
Then,
with your limbs anointed with the sandalwood of ethical discipline, clothed in the mantle of meditative concentration,
and strewn with the flowers of the factors of enlightenment, dwell in happiness as you please. (19)
Having recited this,
one should dismiss [the deities] with: *oṃ vajramaṇḍala muḥ*.
In this manner, one should also worship Mañjuśrī and the others according to the instructions.
The Ritual Procedure for the Mandala Offering.
Generosity is cow dung mixed with water; ethical discipline is sweeping;
patience is the removal of small ants; and vigor is the undertaking of activity.
Meditative concentration is the making of the mind one-pointed at that very moment, and wisdom is its brilliant, well-drawn lines;
by constructing the mandala of the Sage, one obtains these six perfections alone. (20)
He becomes golden-hued, liberated from all diseases, distinguished among gods and men, with a radiant splendor like the moon;
he is born into a royal lineage, enriched with wealth and gold.
Having performed bodily actions within this supreme abode of the Sugata. || 21 ||
Verses on the Praise of the Mandala
Having prepared a mandala every day with flowers, cow dung, and water,
one should offer something to the guru at the three times of the day and pay homage with devotion.
One should avoid causing dissatisfaction in the minds of others for the sake of one's own mind;
being happy, gracious, and fortunate, such a person is born in Sukhāvatī. (23)
He who, perfected in the six pāramitās, empowered by the Buddhas and others, and endowed with infinite virtues, constructs the maṇḍala— [he shall attain success]. (24)
Thus ends the section on the benefits.
Having correctly recited the Prajñāpāramitā according to the ritual procedures for the mandala and so forth, one should constantly worship it and immerse oneself in its meaning. (25)
One should recite the Ekagāthā, the Caturgāthā, the Gāthādvitaya-dhāraṇī, the Ṣaṇmukhī, and the Bhadracaryā at the three times of day. || 26 ||

Beginning with a single syllable and proceeding up to a hundred thousand, the wise person, remaining composed and maintaining his vow without interruption, should recite according to his capacity. (27)
One should also worship paintings, books, images, and so forth of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
|| This is the ritual procedure for the worship of paintings and books. ||
Now, the procedure for the striking of the ritual dagger (*sañcakaṭāḍana*) is extended by analogy according to the *Mahāmaṇḍalavyūha-tantra*.
[The reading *sarvakatāṣanavidhiḥ* in manuscript S is a corruption.]
Homage to all Buddhas!
Oṃ vajrapuṣpe svāhā! This is the mantra for taking the clay. Oṃ vajrodbhavāya svāhā! This is the mantra for the bowing of the image.
Oṃ araje viraje svāhā. This is the mantra for anointing with oil. Oṃ dharmadhātugarbhe svāhā. This is the mantra for casting the mudrā.
Oṃ vajramudgarākoṭana svāhā. This is the mantra for striking.
Oṃ dharmarate svāhā. This is the mantra for summoning. Oṃ supratiṣṭhitavajre svāhā. This is the mantra for consecration.
(Note: *supratiṣṭhita* according to M; *apratiṣṭhita* according to S.)

Oṃ sarvatathāgatamaṇiśatadīpte jvala jvala dharmadhātugarbhe svāhā. This is the consecration mantra (*pratiṣṭhāmantra*). Oṃ svabhāvaśuddhe āhara āhara āgaccha āgaccha dharmadhātugarbhe svāhā. This is the dismissal mantra (*visarjanamantra*).
Oṃ ākāśadhātugarbhe svāhā. This is the mantra for requesting forgiveness. Thus concludes the ritual procedure for striking the *sañcaka*.

*Saṃcakatāḍana*: Oṃ, homage to the Blessed One, Vairocanaprabharāja, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha! It is as follows: Oṃ, subtle one, subtle one; equal one, equanimous one; peaceful one, tamed one; established in composure, without support, O Taraṃbe; O Yaśovatī of great splendor; O Nirvāṇa free from agitation; empowered by the empowerment of all Buddhas, svāhā!
Having recited this dhāraṇī twenty-one times over a lump of clay or a lump of sand, one should fashion a caitya.
As many atoms as there are in that [object], so many millions of caityas are established; one obtains merits equal in number to those atoms,
becomes a lord of the ten stages (*daśabhūmīśvara*), and will swiftly awaken to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment— thus spoke the Blessed One, the Tathāgata Vairocana.
The Dhāraṇī for Bestowing Great Benefits.
Of those phenomena that arise from causes, the Tathāgata has explained their cause, as well as their cessation; such is the teaching of the Great Śramaṇa. (28)

Having established the foundation with this verse, one should perform the worship of the *caitya* with the following: "Oṃ, homage to the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Ratnaketurāja. That is to say: Oṃ ratne ratne mahāratne ratnavijaye svāhā."
By this dhāraṇī, through the veneration of a single caitya, the veneration of ten million caityas is accomplished.
[This concludes] the procedure for constructing caityas from clay, sand, and other materials.
When this is dedicated by means of the most excellent dedication,
it becomes a bringer of an excellent fruit;
one should dedicate it with the great dedication taught in the *Prajñāpāramitā*.

That is to say: just as those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Awakened Ones, through their Buddha-knowledge and Buddha-eye, know and see that root of virtue—its genus, its category, its nature, its characteristics, its intrinsic being, and the reality-principle by which it exists—so do I rejoice in that root of virtue;
and just as those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Awakened Ones authorize it.
"I dedicate that root of merit toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment in such a manner as it is being dedicated.
Furthermore—
By this wholesome deed of mine, may I become a Buddha in this world before long;
may I teach the Dharma for the benefit of all beings.
May I liberate sentient beings who are oppressed by manifold sufferings. || 29 ||
The Procedure for Rejoicing in Merit and the Dedication of Merit.
Whatever means of livelihood each person has that is pure, they should acquire that; they should regard it as one regards medicine for the sake of hunger or for the sake of curing a disease. (30)
For the sake of alms, for the sake of patience;
then, among those who have gathered as they may,
among whatever food has been gathered.
Oṃ, the syllable A is the gateway to all phenomena because they are unarisen from the beginning; Oṃ Āḥ Hūṃ Phaṭ Svāhā.
With this, one should offer the bali.
Oṃ Āḥ, to all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, vajra food offering, Hūṃ!
With this [mantra], one should present the food offering (*naivedya*).
Having recited: *oṃ hārīti mahāyakṣiṇi hara hara sarvapāpān kṣīṃ svāhā*, one should give two balls of food for Hārītī.
Oṃ, svāhā to those who eat the foremost rice-ball!
Thus is the offering of the foremost rice-ball.
Following that, having empowered the food in one's own vessel with "Oṃ Āḥ Hūṃ," as far as...
For the pacification of defects such as poison and the like, one should first touch [water] with the ring finger and thumb and then eat;
this is for the sake of pacification.
Thereafter, having eaten as much as desired, one should offer the leftover food with the mantra:
*oṃ utsṛṣṭapiṇḍāśanebhyaḥ svāhā*, and give the discarded morsel. One should then relinquish the remaining food without any specific intention.
And likewise:
one should offer the bali, the naivedya, Hārītī, and the first piṇḍa.
And one should give the fifth [portion], which has been relinquished for the enjoyment of the great fruit. || 31 ||

Thus, having performed the ritual rinsing of the mouth and so forth, being endowed with a distinguished happiness characterized by purified intellect, one should recite this three times for the sake of the welfare and happiness of all sentient beings.
[He has arrived. He has arrived.
May the king, the patron of the gift, and all other multitudes of sentient beings, always attain happiness, as well as the perfections of long life and health. (32)

Thus, having subsequently purified the actions of body, speech, and mind, he should dwell as he pleases. Immediately thereafter, having sat down, he should pass each day or day after day in conversation with virtuous friends regarding the *nidānas*, *avadānas*, and *jātakas*. [Note: The variant reading in manuscript S is *nidānoktadāna* (gifts mentioned in the *nidānas*).]
Then, at the evening twilight as well, one should perform meditation, recitation, praise, and so forth, with a mind untiring according to one's capacity.
Having offered the bali-oblation with the mantra beginning with *yu-ga-kā-ra*, one should sleep in the yoga-sleep (*yoganidrā*).
How is the term "lay practitioner" (*upāsaka*) to be understood?
Diligently engaged in the worship of the Buddha, he dwells in the tranquility of one who has attained peace.
One should be endowed with skillful means for the sake of benefiting sentient beings. || 33 ||
Thus: One should always avoid evil and association with the most wicked; one should restrain a person from evil and point out sin everywhere. (34)
He should restrain [the mind],
thus;
being free from superimposition and well-composed in meditative absorption.
Always supremely blissful, the wise one shall accomplish perfect enlightenment. || 35 ||
"Ka":
He always exerts effort and maintains compassion;
even through hardship, he does not do what is undesirable, but performs the highest service. (36)
According to this statement:

"This lay practitioner (*upāsaka*), endowed with these four syllables and having accumulated a store of merit by abandoning unwholesome actions, performs only wholesome deeds even in the dream state due to the power of habituation, just as he does in the waking state."
Seeing the world as resembling a reflection—pure and untroubled—one should act toward everything like an illusory person, through non-apprehension. (37)

Therefore, he is called "irreversible. Thus, accumulating a mass of merit continuously and uninterruptedly day and night until reaching the seat of awakening for the sake of the welfare of sentient beings, he shall remain.
By name he is Gaganagarbha, devoted to the meaning of the Middle Way.
Being concentrated, he indeed performs the undertaking of the initial action. || 38 ||
This beginner's practice was performed by me at the request of a noble Brahmin of virtuous intent, who came from Vajrapīṭha. (39)

For here, at the request of Gaganagarbha, I have spoken this "Destruction of the Afflictions" by means of a mere few words, describing the initial stages of practice; having dispelled the darkness of sin, it shall destroy the afflictions.
Before long, through practice, it will lead to enlightenment for one of stainless intellect. || 40 ||
Whatever merit I have obtained by performing this initial rite, may the world obtain the supreme [merit] by performing this initial rite. (41)
The *Kudṛṣṭinirghātana* is completed.
Farewell.
